e: Reduced form of you. Compare Dutch je, reduced/unstressed form of jij (“you”).
Apparently from German ja and cognates in other Germanic languages; related to English yeah.
From Middle English ya, from Old English ġēa, iā (“yea, yes”). More at yea.
q: But you don't really care for music, do ya?

Lola got a shocked look on her face then said, “Ya need to stop actin' jealous if ya aint, and ya can't control what I do. Ya aint my daddy and ya aint my man. I'll see ya tomorrah after work if ya want. Just give me a call, ya have my number”.
2011, Byron Douglas, chapter 3, in A Journey Through the Life of an Anti-Social^([64–65]), →ISBN:
'Ya, wilt thou!' said Wallace, 'then tak thee that, […]'
Ya, auld man, ye ken fine ye wad like me.

e: Contraction of ya + will. By surface analysis, ya (“you”) + 'll.
Contraction of you all or ya all, with spelling perhaps influenced by you'll.
q: Yis, yis; ya'll be forced, or else ya'll tak t' luck awaäy wi' ya, an' that wad niver deä.
1886, Donald MacLeod, editor, Good Words for 1886, page 201:
Bill's spilin' for a fight, / An' one o' these black God-forgotten days / He'll let tha devil tap 'im on tha shoulder, / An' then ya'll see what happens.
Ya'll like that. Ya'll come out smellin like a rose, looking like one, too.
Ya'll only ever be Xavier Cassidy's work horse. He won't treat ya right.
